Initiative: Establish corporate travel policies that prioritise lower carbon transport
Old Initiative: Optimise company travel practices and policies
Description: A formal, written policy that sets clear rules about how staff travels for business, defaulting to lower carbon options and reducing unnecessary travel altogether, rather than leaving travel mode as an individual, ad hoc choice.
Why/Benefit: Transport is one of the largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions, and the carbon impact of different travel modes can vary significantly. A formal travel policy helps employees consistently choose lower-carbon options, reducing business travel emissions without restricting business activity. By prioritising virtual meetings, reducing unnecessary trips, and favouring lower-emission transport modes, organisations can decouple business growth from travel-related emissions and extend sustainable travel practices across suppliers and partners.
How to achieve this: Begin by analysing travel data to identify key emissions hotspots, then establish a clear travel hierarchy that prioritises virtual meetings, rail, public transport, and low-emission vehicles before air travel. Support the policy with practical booking processes, defined approval requirements for exceptions, and measurable travel-emissions KPIs. Regularly review performance and update the policy to reflect changing travel needs and transport options.
Evidence/Case Study: The Culture for Climate Scotland guide explains how organisations should build a sustainable travel policy. It notes transport is the UK's largest emitting sector at roughly 30% of total emissions, and recommends a travel hierarchy from most to least carbon intensive, cars, shared vehicles, public transport, cycling, walking, applied when choosing how to travel. Key recommendations include replacing internal and short-haul flights with rail, avoiding travel altogether where video calls suffice, offering incentives like paid "journey days" for longer sustainable trips, and presenting sustainable versus conventional travel budget options when working with external partners. It also covers staff commuting, cycle to work schemes, flexible working, supplier and delivery choices, and separately addresses audience travel, which it notes is usually an organisation's largest travel emissions source despite sitting outside direct control. The guide closes by pointing to real published policy examples, including WWF UK's and Energy Saving Trust's, as models to reference.
Evidence Reference:
Guide to writing a sustainable travel policy - Culture for Climate Scotland

https://www.ros.gov.uk/about/publications/policy-and-guidelines/2024/green-travel-policy#two
Cost Saving/Cost: Low cost for establishing the policy
Carbon Abatement Potential: Indirect through embedding policy in company day-to-day activities
Time to implement/ROI: Short to medium, roughly 1 to 3 months for the policy itself, longer for full behaviour change.

Initiative: Provide infrastructure and incentives for low-carbon guest travel
Old Initiative: Encourage and enable lower-emission guest travel (e.g. EV charge points, cycling and public transport)
Description: Providing the physical facilities and financial or practical incentives that make it easier for guests to travel to, from, and around a venue using lower carbon transport, rather than defaulting to private car or taxi use.
Why/Benefit: Guest travel is often one of the largest contributors to an organisation's overall carbon footprint, yet it is typically one of the hardest parts for a business to influence directly. Infrastructure and incentives are valuable precisely because they give businesses a genuine, controllable lever over this otherwise indirect source, EV charging points, shuttle services, and rewards for car-free travel all sit within the business's own decisions, rather than depending on guest behaviour alone. Beyond reducing emissions, these measures can enhance the guest experience, attract environmentally conscious customers, and create a competitive advantage that supports both sustainability and commercial objectives. EV charging in particular can generate direct revenue through session-based charging fees, alongside indirect revenue through increased bookings and occupancy from guests who specifically seek out charging access, turning the initiative into a commercial asset rather than a pure cost.
How to achieve this: The approach should be tailored to the site type. Businesses with control over their premises can install EV charging, cycle storage, and public transport signage. Those in leased locations can work with landlords to improve facilities and promote existing transport links. Rural sites may benefit from car-sharing schemes and partnerships with local taxi or shuttle providers, while hotels can offer shared transfers to reduce individual journeys. Infrastructure should be supported by incentives, such as discounts for car-free arrivals or priority access to EV charging, to encourage uptake and maximise impact.

Vineyard Group, a hospitality operator with venues across Hertfordshire and Bedfordshire, replaced free EV charging with a managed pay-as-you-go solution by installing four EV chargers (two 22kW and two 7kW units). The change transformed charging from a cost burden into a revenue-generating amenity, achieving payback in under six months and generating over £6,300 in annual revenue, while also enhancing the guest experience and supporting increased visitor spend and bookings.

https://www.voltshare.co.uk/case-studies
Carbon Abatement Potential:
Forest Holidays, which operates 12 nature-based holiday locations across the UK in partnership with Forestry England, Forestry and Land Scotland, and Natural Resources Wales, deployed 24 EV chargers across 4 of its sites in response to growing guest demand for on-site charging. The rollout delivered over 1,800 charging sessions to 750+ unique users, supplying 49.49 MWh of energy, equivalent to roughly 143,000 EV miles driven, and saving an estimated 26,885 kg of CO2. 

https://www.savemoneycutcarbon.com/project/forest-holidays/

The case study is published by SaveMoneyCutCarbon, the installer behind the project, rather than independently audited, and the reporting period behind the figures isn't stated, so the numbers should be treated as directional rather than a precise annual rate.
Time to implement/ROI: Implementation is typically medium to long term, with timelines ranging from a few weeks for low-cost measures such as travel incentives and signage to nearby  public transport, to 2-6 months for EV charging and cycle storage installations, and 6-12+ months for projects requiring infrastructure upgrades, landlord approvals, or shuttle service deployment. Delivery timelines will vary depending on site ownership, available infrastructure, and electrical capacity.

Initiative: Support and encourage employees in choosing low-carbon commuting alternatives (e.g. cycle to work, public transport)
Old Initiative: Encourage and enable lower-emission employee commuting (e.g. cycle to work, public transport)
Evidence/Case Study: TfL's Smart Commuting Toolkit (2025) recommends reducing employee travel emissions through public transport, active travel, flexible working, and reduced car dependency. Suggested employee incentives include cycle-to-work schemes, bike-share memberships, season ticket loans, flexible/hybrid working, active travel rewards, workplace cycling facilities (showers, lockers, bike parking), travel champions, and car-sharing schemes.
Cost Saving/Cost: TfL's Smart Commuting Toolkit highlights cost savings through reduced parking demand, lower employee commuting costs (bike-share, cycle-to-work schemes, season ticket loans, off-peak travel), and indirect business benefits including improved productivity, fewer sick days, and better staff retention.
Carbon Abatement Potential:
Heathrow Airport's Way2Go app incentivised sustainable commuting through rewards, vouchers and behaviour-change campaigns. By July 2025, the initiative recorded 150,069 sustainable commutes, saved 61,525 kg CO₂e, replaced 80% of solo car trips with sustainable journeys, and encouraged 70% of previously non-sustainable commuters to change travel behaviour.

Initiative: Reduce emissions from delivery and distribution by improving fleet efficiency before the journey
Old Initiative:
Optimise routes for deliveries 
and 
Explore haulage aggregation opportunities
How to achieve this:
1. Load & Route Planning: Right-size vehicles to actual load, and plan routes and loads together using route planning software or a logistics provider that sequences stops efficiently.
2. Shared Logistics: Explore haulage aggregation with other businesses, sharing truck space and routes so vehicles carry more, more often.
3. Vehicle Transition: Transition fleet to EVs or low-carbon fuel vehicles at natural end of service life, not early replacement, and install EV charging infrastructure at depots to support this.
4. Temperature controlled goods: Optimise cold chain and refrigerated transport, minimising stops and door-open time, consolidating loads, and prioritising electric or cryogenic refrigeration units over diesel.
5. Drive behaviour: Train drivers in smooth acceleration, reduced idling, and consistent route adherence.

Initiative: Reduce emissions from delivery and distribution by improving fleet efficiency during and after the journey
How to achieve this:
1. Return Journey: Use the return journey for backhauling, carrying recycling, reusable packaging, or containers back to source rather than running empty.
2. Vehicle Monitoring: Install telematics and a digital asset management system to track fuel use, idling time, and vehicle condition in real time, and feed this data back into fleet decisions to catch maintenance issues early.
3. Delivery Timing: Schedule deliveries to avoid road congestion, ideally paired with route optimisation software.

Initiative: Reduce emissions from delivery and distribution by engaging with suppliers
How to achieve this:
1. Procurement Consolidation: Centralise procurement across sites through a single system or department, consolidating orders to reduce delivery frequency, and favour suppliers offering efficient local delivery.
2. Supplier Engagement: Strengthen supplier relationship management, using regular engagement to request consolidated deliveries, emissions data, or lower-carbon transport options directly.
3. Delivery Consolidation: Ask suppliers to consolidate your deliveries with other nearby customers on the same route, rather than sending a dedicated part-load.
4. Order Timing: Apply just-in-time delivery principles with caution, balanced against consolidation, since tightly-timed delivery can increase emissions by disrupting efficient routing.
5. Demand Forecasting: Use data analytics to forecast demand and track supplier performance, reducing both waste and emissions-heavy urgent orders.
